Coach was ‘transparent’ in dealings with club, federation

Pochettino had signed deal to stay with US through 2030

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.

“These moments are not easy decisions,” a reflective Pochettino told the media. “Normally it’s the opposite. Normally you get sacked and you cry because you want to stay and you’re sacked by [the club]. It’s a tough decision but at the same time we are excited for the next step forward.”

Pochettino characterized United’s interest and negotiations as having come together at the last minute, essentially, with contact between the two sides first made Sunday.

“We cannot underestimate the staff and the players. When things became big and big and big, the players are very sensitive and the staff are too – they start to feel things as well. [Everything] was so quick, because we arrived here last Friday and Sunday afternoon this situation started to appear and some contact. We were very transparent, we were talking with [US Soccer CEO] JT [Batson] and the federation.”

Details were quickly ironed out between the sides, with the club and federation agreeing Pochettino would remain with the US through the upcoming matches.

“[Thursday], when things were positive in the way the agreement was, we had a meeting and I communicated to the players and the whole staff. I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation and they know us – how committed we are for the next two games. The decision between the federation and Manchester United , to agree that we’ll continue with our job in the camp; [nothing] can change our commitment and how important the next two games are.”

Pochettino and the US federation touted his contract renewal in August as the start of something new and significant, with the coach given a larger role in the overall direction of the US men at every level. That went by the wayside when United came knocking.

“They know that there are not too many opportunities that can happen in your career like [this one with Manchester United],” Pochettino said. “When they arrive, it’s difficult to turn down. But I want to make it clear, when we decided together to [stay another four years], it was always the commitment for the federation, too. Maybe the four games [in the September/October window] if we lose them, maybe you start to put pressure [on me]. And maybe something can be in a different way.

“Or even in the future,” he continued, “Things can happen. The federation and maybe new people arrive or don’t, or maybe have different ideas and you say, ‘We are thinking in different directions’ and maybe they say ‘Mauricio, maybe you need to go home.’ We cannot think in these extremes – I think we were very committed and never thought this would happen so quickly.”

Pochettino was joined by Batson and US Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone on Friday. Batson was pressed on what will happen with the approximately $10m (£7.5m) Manchester United paid out for Pochettino’s services. A significant portion of Pochettino’s $6m salary was subsidized by billionaire hedge fund manager and US Soccer donor Ken Griffin. It’s unclear whether that generosity will extend towards Pochettino’s successor.

“The agreement with Manchester United, those funds – as you all know, US Soccer is a nonprofit and those funds are used to help us hire great coaches,” Batson said. “They help us do youth national team programs, coaching education … those funds are available for us to invest in order for us to make the biggest impact on our goals. Our supporters, our sponsors, our donors, are fans are very supportive around making sure that we have the resources that we need to achieve our goals, including having a world-class coach. We are appreciative of that support and look forward to our way of winning going forwards.”

Pochettino’s legacy, of course, is still to be defined. He was by no means a generational influence on the state of soccer in the US but he will be remembered fondly, by many, for a handful of standout performances and for guiding the US to a respectable, albeit disappointing, last-16 finish at this summer’s World Cup.

Pochettino was reluctant at first to define his own legacy, telling reporters he was “not arrogant” before jokingly conceding that he is “well, a little bit arrogant, but not too much.”

“We don’t take a project to be remembered forever,” Pochettino said, “and to have a picture here at the training center. It’s the impact on the human being. It’s for us to be a good partner and, through the vision of the federation, to add our quality and knowledge of the game and to be part of this family. I hope, in Manchester United, to do the same. That is what we can do – add our expertise about soccer … The key factor, though, that can have a key influence is the human being.”

items.lbText:
Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches

He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract

Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

United made Pochettino their first-choice target after it became clear Carrick would be dismissed. They only held talks with the Argentinian, despite interest in the former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann. United’s leadership group selected Pochettino over other candidates and had the decision to appoint him signed off by Sir Jim Ratcliffe this week.

The club were attracted to Pochettino based on his personality, hoping he can turn things around at United by building a strong culture within the dressing room. United sought a more experienced coach after Carrick, feeling Pochettino’s long-term record of player development and clear philosophy would suit the needs of United at the moment.

Pochettino signed a new four-year contract with US Soccer in August, an expansive deal that offered the Argentinian greater control over youth development and the overall direction of the men’s programme. To secure his services, United have paid the US federation about $10m (£7.5m), with an additional fee paid to secure the services of Pochettino’s longtime assistants.

United’s players not on international duty were told on Thursday they did not need to return to training until next week. With the second of the US’s two games against Haiti finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, Pochettino’s first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

“The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country,” Pochettino said on Friday.

“We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.”

Pochettino was hired by US Soccer in September 2024, brought on to steer the US through their first home World Cup in 32 years. Over the ensuing two years he compiled a 21-12-2 record and guided the team to the World Cup last 16, results that stack up favourably alongside other US coaches.

He earned praise in the US for his enthusiasm and for putting together the US men’s greatest group stage at a World Cup, a performance that included a 4-1 dismantling of Paraguay that will go down as the team’s best 90-minute performance at the tournament. All of that early progress, though, was wiped out by a 4-1 loss to Belgium in the last 16, a result marred by the federation’s – and Pochettino’s – handling of the red card controversy surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun.

It was not his only lowlight: there was the shocking fourth-place finish in the 2024-25 Nations League and a bitterly disappointing loss to Mexico in the 2025 Gold Cup final. The US were thrashed by top-level competition in friendly matches, and Pochettino sometimes struggled to connect with players, primarily the Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic. Others, such as Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie, found themselves in and out of the picture on a regular basis.

Pochettino leaves the US with a glimmer of hope for the future. Across his tenure, 75 players earned at least one cap for the US. In the months after signing his extension, he did well to integrate more than a dozen newcomers into the squad during a four-match international window during which the US went undefeated across four matches.

Steve Cherundolo, head coach of the US U-23 national team, will lead the senior team’s December camp, which will feature a roster of primarily Major League Soccer players.

United’s captain, Bruno Fernandes, has rejected a second offer of a new contract but the club are confident of getting the midfielder to commit his future. The 32-year-old’s deal runs until the end of the season but United have the option to trigger a further year.

Fernandes would be allowed to speak to clubs abroad in January if United have not activated that clause. He has previously had interest from Saudi Arabia and Galastasaray.

Fernandes won the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s player of the year award last season after helping United to third in the league with a record-breaking 21 assists but his form has dipped. He took aim at Carrick’s tactics after last month’s defeat by Como in the Champions League.

“A s a United fan who was around for the early 90s seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation. He was the only likable thing about the club … I took my eight-year-old lad to Old Trafford for the Brighton game in the FA Cup in January and I’ve never experienced a more toxic atmosphere at a football ground. The fans deserve better … Better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment” – Chris

“Wilcox, [Berada] and [Jim] Ratcliffe should have fired themselves. They are the common denominator of all this failure. [Mauricio] Pochettino will last 12 months if he’s lucky” – Deb

“I have been a United supporter for over 60 years and this sacking just depresses me. Everyone knows the problem lies elsewhere … We were in desperate need of a left-back and centre-half. What did they do? Recruit several midfielders. So it starts again. Does anyone really believe changing manager will make any difference?” – Barry

“This feels sadder than every other time it’s happened since Alex Ferguson retired. Each of the previous managers had to go, as in large part the underperformance felt like it was their fault. This doesn’t feel like that … But, because the owners and executives aren’t going to sack themselves, and because you can’t fire the players, you change the only thing you can: the manager. And then repeat the cycle” – John

“I think it was Jonathan Liew who made the eminently sensible suggestion of a positional switch for Michael Carrick – by having him replace Jason Wilcox as director of football. That would have made sense” – Geoff

“Just waiting for Mr Mediocrity Wilcox to do the honourable thing and admit he is out of his depth and responsible in part for the situation and resign” – Andrew

“Since Fergie left there have been 12 managers at United, including interims, with little reward. Can all of these have been wrong? Surely they could not have been? It highlights the systemic failures of the club at all levels” – Simon

“Carrick remains a Manchester United legend, he will always be. Without corresponding changes in the club’s recruitment process and the people driving it, we will be back here after 12-18 months” – Wale

“There are many problems at United but the biggest is short-termism. Carrick, like Ole Gunnar Solskjær, was given the permanent job because he did a good job as caretaker, but those roles are very different. Building for the long term, even at a well-run club with solid foundations, is different from getting the best from the hand you’ve been dealt over a few months. Since Fergie retired managers have been sacked because results have taken a downturn, and those who’ve suggested things might need to get worse before they get better (Ralf Rangnick and Ruben Amorim) have been shown the door. There are no reasons to think it will be any different for Pochettino” – Jason

“Is Pochettino a good manager? He did well at Spurs – albeit without winning anything – and in a short spell at Southampton but that was a long time ago. Since then his record has been pretty underwhelming, up to and including an uninspiring time in charge of the US men’s team. He just seems to have a reputation as a good manager but I’m not really sure what it’s based on any more” – Jon

“The similarities between ENIC’s ownership of Tottenham and the Glazers stewardship of United are striking. It doesn’t bode well for United given Tottenham’s unprecedented two-and-a-half decades of underachievement since then. The main difference, further bad news for United, is that Tottenham’s perilous debt load primarily funded a new stadium rather than facilitating the owners’ stake in the company and subsequent dividends to themselves. Football clubs can’t withstand money being extracted – it all has to be re-invested to keep the wheels turning” – Paul

“In 53 years of supporting United this is the most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years. The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they see winning as nice to have [but] not the core objective of an elite football club … I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. It was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail and fail quickly. Our first team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us? It doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue” – Robert

“I have supported United for over 70 years through thick and thin but no more, to support United means supporting the Glazers. And I just wonder would a fans’ boycott get rid of them. An empty Old Trafford might do it” – Paul

“I am 62. I have followed Manchester United since the age of four (I found a picture of George Best, and told my mum I liked him). I stood on the Stretford End in my teens and took my son during the 90s. The fanbase needs to wrest control. The only way this will change is for the fanbase to boycott games. Stop going, stop providing matchday revenue. If the Glazers are only interested in the money, stop providing them with an income” – Bob…

Argentinian oversaw high-scoring games in his one Chelsea season and Opta predicts his Manchester United side will move upfield quicker than that team

A mong the 20 managers with more than 290 matches in the Premier League, only the five “ big beasts ” of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Mauricio Pochettino. He is an elite manager.

Pochettino took over Southampton midway through their first season back in the top flight (2012-13) after the club spent seven years in the lower leagues. In his only full campaign, they finished eighth. He led Tottenham to second in 2016-17, third in the seasons either side, and reached the 2019 Champions League final . His presence lifted those clubs.

However, the Argentinian has competed in only one of the past six Premier League campaigns. Winning Ligue 1 and the Coupe de France in an 18-month spell with Paris Saint-Germain tells us little. His most pertinent recent experience for the Manchester United job is the 2023-24 season he spent at Chelsea, a campaign that left more questions than answers.

The club had finished 12th the season before, in the first year of the Todd Boehly/Clearlake Capital era. Pochettino was always likely to take Chelsea higher. And he did. But his influence is harder to judge. Opta predicted Chelsea would finish sixth in 2023-24, a forecast that proved correct. By this measure Pochettino hit par though, as Transfermarkt rated the market value of his squad as the third-highest in the Premier League in October 2023, perhaps he fell short.

The squad value grew thanks to remarkable investment. Chelsea spent more than any other club in Europe’s big five leagues in each of the three transfer windows from the summer of 2022 to the summer of 2023. Working for Boehly will have provided a good primer for the madness of Manchester United, even if the spending won’t be as generous.

Assembling a winning team from a rapidly evolving squad is not easy. Pochettino crafted a side that delivered the fifth-most expected points in 2023-24. Chelsea’s 63.4 was a fair way shy of Arsenal (81.2), Manchester City (79.3) and Liverpool (76.2) but it was a decent first season.

Chelsea conceded 63 league goals, the club’s worst figure in the Premier League era. Yet only twice have they amassed more than the 77 goals they scored. They were a little above their expected goal figures at each end but the bulk of their large goal totals was reflected in the underlying data.

But even the xG numbers raised questions, because Chelsea benefited from 12 penalties, the joint-second-most in the past 10 Premier League seasons. Chelsea have had 14 in their 86 league games since Pochettino left. They conceded five penalties and committed the joint-most Opta-defined defensive errors leading to shots (22) in Pochettino’s season.

Across three matches in April 2024 they drew 2-2 with the bottom side Sheffield United, thumped Everton 6-0 then lost 5-0 at Arsenal. They endured a similar seesaw sequence earlier in the campaign, losing 4-1 at Tottenham and Newcastle, with a 4-4 draw against Manchester City in between. Chelsea also set the record for matches in which a team score and concede at least two goals in a 38-game Premier League season (12). How do you assess a manager’s performance in that maelstrom?

If the low point was not the Arsenal loss, it was being called “ billion-pound bottle jobs ” by Gary Neville after losing the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Never mind that Chelsea had enough chances to win, Pochettino had to answer for the defeat. Less than three months later, he was gone.

The Premier League has evolved in Pochettino’s relatively brief absence. Arne Slot arrived, won the title and left, while Guardiola’s departure leaves no big managerial beasts remaining. There have been tactical shifts, with increased man-to-man marking across the pitch, and set-piece skirmishes have decided more matches than feels healthy.

Opta’s data shows Pochettino’s probable new side move upfield more quickly but press less intensely than his Chelsea team. There will need to be an adjustment. But can a manager whose training methods at Chelsea were described by a well-placed source as “antiquated” get up to speed as quickly as United need?

Pochettino will adapt and his Premier League record commands the utmost respect. The relevance of his recent work to United in 2026-27 is less clear.

items.title: Carrick sacked by Manchester United with team in Premier League relegation zone – as it happened
items.author: John Brewin; Luke McLaughlin and John Ashdown
items.content:
The latest news and reaction as Manchester United look for a new head coach after only only three victories so far this season

“After going through the Moyes season,” writes Hugh, “the dross football of Mourinho and Van Gaal, the moments-years of Solskjaer, the Rangnick surgery that never was, the middling Ten Hag, the baffling Amorim, and now a decent man thrust into the meat grinder, this is the first year it’s been genuinely hard to watch Man Utd with any emotion.

“And it’s not because of the football. It’s that the Glazer ownership and Ratcliffe mismanagement has met the Man City revelations, meaning it’s hard to see the point anymore. £1bn taken out of the club while others were illicitly pumping in roughly the same. A club drained of life, hollowed out … I can take crap football, but I can’t take this anymore.”

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) earlier issued a statement following Carrick’s dismissal pinning the blame for poor results firmly on the ownership. In full below:

Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager.

The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.

But the discontent at United is not just about matters on the pitch. Far from it.

Aggressive ticketing policies have further damaged relations with supporters. Treating loyal fans principally as a source of revenue undermines their identity and the bond with the team that sustains support through difficult times. Supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights.

The earlier Stretford End banner declaring “The way you treat us is a disgrace” was a warning. The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.

MUST warned publicly in January 2025 that alienating supporters risked a downward spiral of worsening atmosphere, performances and financial outcomes. Our subsequent Telegraph article urged Sir Jim Ratcliffe to break that “doom loop” by bringing supporters with him. Those warnings remain painfully relevant.

The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success. Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.

items.lbText:
Michael Carrick’s replacement must find solutions on the pitch and pressure the hierarchy to accept a share of blame

One of the final images of Michael Carrick’s time in charge will be of him standing in the rain on the Old Trafford touchline watching his side succumb to Bournemouth , while his sullen captain sat unused on the bench. Bruno Fernandes was dropped after calling out his head coach’s tactics, although Carrick said it was for football reasons. It was the second combustible television interview in as many Champions League games after Lisandro Martínez pointed the finger at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, for failing to provide a squad suitable for fighting on all fronts.

Fernandes was soon back in the fold, and Martínez apologised for his outburst , but it is clear internal discipline is an issue and will be central to getting the team back on track. United will always draw more attention than almost any other club in the world and creating a circus around a failing team merely complicates matters when there are already enough problems to sort out on the pitch. The players need to harness their anger to ensure they create headlines for performances, not interviews.

One player Jason Wilcox could claim as a recruitment success was Senne Lammens but the goalkeeper’s form has joined that of his teammates in the gutter. The Belgian endured a horror show for Bournemouth’s third goal when he rushed out of his area, and he made two errors in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa . Leny Yoro was another to make a terrible mistake against Bournemouth, while Diogo Dalot’s efforts as a makeshift left-back can be categorised as somewhere between woeful and inept. No team in Europe’s top five leagues have conceded more than United’s 30 in all competitions, which is clearly a worry.

Morale is at rock bottom but the chopping and changing in defence is creating more uncertainty. The new head coach should pick a back four and stick with it where possible. If Harry Maguire’s experience is deemed mandatory, he needs pace around him to make up for what he lacks. Luke Shaw’s absence has created a left-back tombola as Dalot, Ayden Heaven and Noussair Mazraoui have been placed there.

Benjamin Sesko’s injury has cost United a No 9 for most of the season and Joshua Zirkzee has rarely been trusted in the role. Matheus Cunha gave it a go as a false 9 and Bryan Mbeumo was tried as a more traditional centre-forward but without much success either. Cunha has become more productive in a deeper role behind the striker, cutting in from the left as he did at Wolves, but United require someone to be a classic No 9, someone who can occupy defenders and be serviced by deliveries from wide. Zirkzee, for his faults, has been a presence when used in recent weeks and scored against Aston Villa. If a new coach can rebuild his confidence, the Dutchman could provide a short-term solution. Alternatively, greater demands should be made of Marcus Rashford to play through the middle.

A mix-and-match of expletives were aimed at those above Carrick at recent home games. Wilcox has taken most of the individual criticism, but the ownership were told in no uncertain terms to sell up. The Glazers have been instrumental in driving the club downwards in recent years and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s investment and involvement in football operations have yielded little success.

Carrick was the face of the operation, as the new head coach will be, and he needs to put pressure on someone at the top to speak to the media to explain why the club is in such a mess because it is unfair to expect the coach to do so. United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.

Three central midfielders and a backup goalkeeper did not make for an inspiring summer when everyone knew United’s squad required improvement in numerous positions. Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans started together against Bournemouth and offered no evidence for why so much was spent on them.

Whoever comes in needs to be clear about what is required, whether in the winter or summer windows, because the deficiencies in the squad mean United cannot compete on all fronts and are struggling to cope with the rigours of the Premier League. A new left-back and striker are a given, but there is plenty more work to be done.

Outrunning the opposition does not guarantee success but United have looked pedestrian on far too many occasions this season. This could explain the number of slow starts to games in recent times: in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid and Como they conceded in the first and second minute respectively, and were two down at home to Roma after 17 minutes last week. Worse still, Aston Villa, aided by errors, were two goals ahead within four minutes at Old Trafford, giving United a monumental task to turn things around. The players deserve credit for finding some fight to do so but need to make life easier for themselves because it does not take a genius to work out starting with a deficit is ill-advised. They will face a fiery atmosphere at Anfield, and that will be a fine place to show a shift in dynamic.

USMNT coach agreed framework of a deal with United

United have made contact with US federation

Balogun: ‘I’d like to keep things the way they are’

Live news and reaction for Pochettino’s move to Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino will lead the US men’s national team through the remainder of this international window, a source with direct knowledge of US Soccer’s plans told the Guardian on Thursday.

Pochettino has emerged as the leading candidate to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked as Manchester United manager on Thursday. The Guardian previously reported that the framework of a deal had been agreed between Pochettino and United. The Athletic was first to report news of Pochettino’s plans for the upcoming US matches.

The USMNT face Haiti on Saturday and then again on Tuesday in Miami and Cincinnati, respectively, in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf Nations League. Pochettino has been leading the US through training at the federation’s headquarters and training facility outside Atlanta this week. The Argentinian has yet to publicly address his link to United, though he is scheduled to speak to reporters on Friday morning.

United have also officially made contact with US Soccer in an approach for Pochettino’s services, multiple sources familiar with the negotiations said Thursday. Pochettino and his representatives had already ironed out details of a proposed agreement, with the Argentinian keeping the federation appraised of those ongoing talks. United would need to pay a buyout clause of $10m (£7.5m) to hire Pochettino and millions more, reportedly, to bring along his longtime assistant coaching staff, who are also expected to make the move.

At US training this week, Pochettino’s players have addressed the still-fluid situation surrounding their head coach. Striker Folarin Balogun told reporters on Thursday that “If I had a vote, I’d like to keep things the way they are.”

On Tuesday, defender Antonee Robinson downplayed the significance of Pochettino’s reported departure.

“As a soccer player, we’re pretty used to sort of fast training environments and games … so we’re all very good at just focusing on the next task and about the next session or the next game coming up,” Robinson said. “For me personally, I don’t really look at it … It’s just focusing on we’ve got a game at the weekend and I’m going to do everything I can to be ready to play for him, and how he wants us to play.”

items.lbText:
Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

F or a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking , consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata . Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como .

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United .

items.lbText:
Club pay tribute to ‘legend’ but say change ‘necessary’

Pochettino in line to take two USA games before leaving

Mauricio Pochettino is poised to sign a deal to take over at Manchester United after Michael Carrick was sacked as the head coach with the team in the Premier League’s ­relegation zone.

Pochettino was on Thursday discussing the final details to join a club with one win from their past 11 matches. He will lead the USA for the last time in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final games against Haiti on Saturday and on Tuesday and should be at Carrington next week to prepare United to face Liverpool at Anfield in their first match after the international break. With the second US game finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, his first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

United have been in contact with US Soccer to extricate Pochettino from a contract that runs to 2030. The former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea manager has a release clause of about $10m (£7.5m) and United will have to pay more to take his staff.

Carrick’s departure comes with United third from bottom of the Premier League, a point behind 17th-placed Coventry, and 17th in the Champions League standings. It follows a review led by the ­director of football, Jason Wilcox, and a ­recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy. Wilcox and United’s chief executive, Omar ­Berrada, travelled to Monaco to meet Ratcliffe .

Carrick’s sacking was then signed off at a board meeting involving the Glazer family. Carrick turned up for work on Thursday morning – as he has done each day this week – with his fate in effect sealed. No further training will be held until next week.

United said: “After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions. Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of ­dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.”

Eddie Howe, out of a job since leaving Newcastle in July , had been on Wilcox’s radar as a replacement for Carrick, while the former Germany and Bayern Munich coach Julian Nagelsmann was the initial choice of Christopher Vivell, the director of recruitment. But United have targeted Pochettino, who left Chelsea in May 2024 and took the USA job four months later .

Carrick was given the job in May on a contract to 2028 after a successful interim spell during which he secured Champions League qualification. He won 12 and drew three of his 17 games last season, but has been unable to continue that trend.

United have three victories so far this season in all competitions – at home to Ipswich, Sabah and Roma. They twice fought back from two goals down last Sunday to salvage a late point in a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa , after a dramatic recovery to beat Roma 3-2 , but the club concluded a change was needed.

Carrick was allowed three games after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth to prove he remained the right person for the job, but United felt after the performances against Chelsea , where they lost 2-0, Roma (won 3-2) and Villa (4-4) that they were on the wrong path and that another coach could get far more from the squad. They consider 18th place in the Premier League unacceptable.

The sacking continues a period of turmoil at United also marked by Bruno Fernandes challenging Carrick’s strategy after a 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como and Lisandro Martínez criticising Wilcox.

Since Sir Alex Ferguson left in 2013 the club have appointed eight managers, including Ralf Rangnick, who had a five-month interim spell. Carrick is the second head coach fired by United in one calendar year, after Ruben Amorim went in January, a first for the club.

items.title: Meeting of two lost souls: can Pochettino make it work at Manchester United? | Barney Ronay

items.content:
Manager has been hurt by experiences at elite clubs but several players at Old Trafford could fit his playing style

Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here.

Manager has been hurt by experiences at elite clubs but several players at Old Trafford could fit his playing style

W elcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino . United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here.

By now Pochettino has been thoroughly processed through the soul-extraction machinery of elite club football. He arrives at Old Trafford pre-minced, pre‑haunted, a 54-year-old already bruised by his experiences at Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and Levy‑era Spurs. This is a head coach so steeped in the blood of dysfunctional super-clubs that turning back is pretty much the same thing as heading on into its ultimate form in the west end of Manchester.

The problems at Old Trafford are of course unrelated to the appointment of the latest managerial avatar. The constant hiring and firing is a symptom not a cause. This is essentially a distraction, a false flag drawing attention from the avarice and incompetence of the executive tiers.

Still, though, it is necessary on these occasions to set out the reasons why the latest appointment probably won’t work. First up is the obvious sense of diminishing returns.

How do you solve a club that has won two major trophies in 10 years of steady downward progress? Easy. You hire a coach who has also won two major trophies in 13 years of steady downward progress. How do we get back to the dimly remembered recent past? We hire the dimly remembered recent past.

Does this feel like a magic bullet? At this stage hiring Pochettino is like booking the bloke who did Gangnam Style to play the Super Bowl. Yeah, huge fan. Remind me. Weren’t you quite big in 2013?

So much for all that then. It is more interesting to linger on the fact that, as ever with this great belching toxic volcano of a football club, there is always hope, and some kind of logic that says maybe this is the one. We see it every time. Ageing aura-master? Yep, do it. Hot young systems zealot? Get him in. Random ex-player, who will be transformed almost instantly into a damp, doomed figure crumpled on the touchline like a divorced dad at the school railings? We have a vacancy.

This time there are two things in Pochettino’s favour. First, the memory of his best days at Tottenham: the charisma, the barking laugh, the way of striding around looking like the world’s most handsome oil rigger. Plus of course the visceral, hard-running style of that early Spurs team, football as life, pain, exhaustion, delirium. There will be moments. Just give us some of these. In the end everyone here just wants to feel something.

Second, and more seductive, is the sense of some kind of shared redemption arc, a union of lost souls. Broken club, meet broken manager. You two are going to get along. This happens in movies, the Leaving Las Vegas dynamic: rock bottom, healing, redemption. Is this convincing? Do we have, of all things, not hope – obviously not that – but doomed hope?

Pochettino does have an incompleteness to his career. This is a manager who never manifested the full promise of those early years, headhunted by Southampton, then poached again by Spurs, where he offered a compelling injection of energy. That Pochettino was a hugely moreish figure. You wanted to hear him speak, clap his dimpled cheeks, to breathe in his Eau de Gaucho scent as he whispered gruff words in your ear about struggle and suffering, and maybe invited you to a barbecue later.

A decade on, Pochettino still has the air of someone looking for a home and a final form. It is an interesting exercise just trying to decide what really broke him. Maybe it was PSG, January 2021 to July 2022, still the source of his only major trophies.

In Paris Pochettino seemed to arrive pre-burnt out, required to make sense from a standing start of a bunch of supernova galácticos . This was High Decadence-era PSG, source of the original despot‑general Kylian Mbappé meme, and a time when Neymar seemed to be more or less continually dancing on crutches in an elite underground disco dressed in a solid gold bowler hat and shoes made from moon rock.

Those who know Pochettino reported a disillusionment with superstar egotism, the swagger of unproven young players, training that became a losing battle for intensity. And yes, there is a pre‑United klaxon here. How’s that going to work out? Does it seem like an obvious cultural fit?

Then again, maybe it was Chelsea that broke him, an ill-fitting season before a mutually agreed departure, shot through with frustration at an unbalanced squad and an incoherent hierarchy. Again, does this sound like a man ideally geared to make sense of a squad assembled under six managers and the interventions of pub-chat Big Sir Jim?

You could even make a case it was Spurs that broke Pochettino, even if for five seasons this was his peak time in club management. The good times died at Tottenham because Pochettino couldn’t convince Daniel Levy of the need to build from a point of strength. That team was destined to eat itself. Pochettino was high on the Marcelo Bielsa school of football as a game of running, victory as a function of physical and emotional exhaustion.

In the end the thing that made Poch-era Spurs work was also the thing that killed it, a high-energy team that became a zombified entity, a squad of degraded parts, Pochettino himself already a little sad and war-weary.…

The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died aged 69 . Kelly edited the NME and Q Magazine and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer. Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

In many ways the role as the new fall guy for Big Sir Jim/the Tampa Bay Glazers (delete as per owner-shambles preference) will suit Mauricio Pochettino if he is given the Manchester United job . He has a reputation as an underdog. A man who has taken on the challenges of managing upstart PSG, tough-times-make-tough-people Chelsea and most recently the soccer team of the most powerful nation on earth, is used to working with his hands tied behind his back (albeit presumably resting on the significant wedge in a nearby pocket).

There are at least some transferable skills Pochettino can bring with him from the USA USA USA: extracting performances from creaking defenders; managing the expectations of a fanbase with outsized ambitions given the quality of talent available for selection; and working in an environment where an egotistical billionaire is known for making unhelpful noises about immigration. Should Pochettino soon be packing up his desk at the Arthur M Blank US Soccer National Training Center (1x tie, lightly stained; 1x white shirt, still in packaging; 1x jacket, no matching trousers; 1x maté cup, unwashed; 1x framed photo of Sansa the dog, regularly dusted; 1x Spurs-branded stress ball, heavily used) it would come at a very awkward time.

Pochettino did not invent sacking the Manchester United manager during the November international break, but he did say within the last few months that he wanted to “have a lasting impact” in the US. Then there is the small matter of his name on a four-year contract extension signed in August. It seems his lasting impact will be a jilted feeling. USA USA USA play Haiti on Saturday, but by then Pochettino could be settling in at the Lowry hotel and turning his mind to whether or not he removes ketchup from the training-ground canteen. In addition to the last-minute rate United will be paying at one of Manchester’s plushest hotels, axing Michael Carrick and getting Pochettino out of his US Soccer deal will cost in the region of £10m.

It is unclear at this stage if there are any more “efficiencies” to make at Carrington, but perhaps if the club’s top brass would stop shooting themselves in the foot they could save a few pennies by not having to repair the damage to the floor. Pochettino was once the perfect candidate to return United to glory. That was seven years and six managers ago. His time at Chelsea was not happy, but he did an admirable job and he is probably the first United candidate since José Mourinho to evidently have what it takes to manage “at this level”. But the big question is: what will Pochettino wear on the touchline for his next big adventure? There’s a partially real but very enticing prospect of him giving soon-to-be jungle inhabitant Wayne Rooney a job in his backroom staff so they can wear matching outfits. What a thought.

The FSA Awards are fast approaching folks and, though Football Daily has been cruelly overlooked yet again, Big Website has been nominated for a gong as well as Football Weekly, Women’s Football Weekly and Suzanne Wrack. If you want to show your support by casting a vote, you can here .

“When my grandfather died many years ago he said the only thing he wanted was to be buried next to Barça’s pitch so that he could hear the goals go in during the afterlife. Many fans dream of the same thing” – María Elena Fort, a Barcelona vice-president, reveals they are living up to their Més que un club motto by providing 26,000 niches where fans can deposit their loved ones’ ashes after the final, final whistle. A lovely gesture – with prices starting at only €2,490 for a 10-year lease. Hmm, what happens when the time’s up?

Re: managers and technical areas ( yesterday’s Football Daily letters ). I do not want to hear about or see Mikel Arteta’s logs; I suggest that, rather than have a technical area, a post is placed on the sideline. Each manager would be attached by a bungee to this so they could not go on to the pitch. Each post would be placed so that opposing managers would, at full extent, be kept an arm’s length from each other. An extension of this could include replacing a yellow card for managers with a shortening of their bungee. A second red would result in no bungee, just being shackled to the post” – Ron Buzzacott.

Can I recommend the flamin’ A-League? Managers from Perth to Brisbane are routinely forced to perform an awkward high-step/half-jump if they want to get over the bumpers that stand between them and the pitch. Don’t worry, they haven’t forgotten to slather these containment devices with adverts” – Patrick Connolly.

John Holtom’s missive (Monday’s letters) about the pitch drop experiment must be the most Noble Francis letter not actually written by Noble Francis. I read the first two sentences and immediately scrolled down to be surprised with a new name. Is Noble Francis becoming a Guardiola-like figure in Football Daily letter-writing? Influencing generations to come?” – Kristian Karamfiles.

I enjoyed Ramon Vega’s Fifa push ( yesterday’s Quote of the Day ). Stirring stuff. However, am I alone in wondering whether maybe given recent history, a non-Swiss might be a wiser choice for the next Fifa head-honcho?” – Andrew Parker.…

The former Tottenham manager is always going to be a subject of interest, but United’s job carries a rare power

As Mauricio Pochettino left the podium to close his final press conference of the last international window, he offered an ambiguous farewell.

“See you next …” Pochettino began as he headed to the tunnels of Allianz Field in Saint Paul, before cutting his sentence short. Then, a bit of a sing-song: “See you next, see you next.”

You don’t need an AI clanker’s autocomplete function to try closing the sentence. “See you next month” would have been synonymous with “see you next window”, after all. Still, the farewell felt poignant given questions about whether Pochettino was going to last a full four-year cycle as US men’s national team head coach.

In hindsight, maybe he had omitted adding something along the lines of: see you next, before I’m off to my next project .

From the moment that Pochettino and US Soccer announced his contract renewal in August, it was tough for many to imagine he would don his lavish safari shirts on the US sideline at the 2030 World Cup. This was Mauricio Pochettino , after all, a name brand in club management whose résumé teemed with unfinished business. Few great coaches hang their hat on being Premier League and Champions League runners-up.

Gone are the days where clubs with major financial considerations pull the plug on a whim. The time to strike is now at the start of an international window, when the next game isn’t for another couple of weeks. This serves as a crucial time to meet the squad, put them through their paces and hatch an initial scheme to stop the rot.

That puts international federations like US Soccer in an unenviable position. Pochettino is among the most eligible options for the Big Clubs, ensuring his continuing presence on managerial wishlists. And as long as that remains the case, the most likely window for advances from club suitors will be right in the stretch of time where a national team coach works hardest.

In September, that meant reheating years-old discourses about the apparent irresistibility of Tottenham Hotspur . Before the World Cup, Milan had come calling . And now, the focus turns to Old Trafford.

The attraction is logical. For over a decade, United have tested every managerial archetype possible since Sir Alex Ferguson called time on his illustrious career. Domestic options who punched above their weight class; chronic winners; onetime supernovas, with implosion all but inevitable; club legends; club custodians; young options ready for a Premier League closeup. Their tenures all ended the same.

Pochettino blends some of the best traits of Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho with a record of doing the work United hoped would happen under Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. His work building Tottenham into a threat on all fronts bolstered his culture-building cachet, showing his success at Espanyol and Southampton could scale. Even though his time at Paris Saint-Germain failed to yield their long-coveted Champions League title, he had experienced managing the egos of Neymar, Mbappé and Messi. Chelsea tested his tolerance for ownership-meddling. All of these factors inform Manchester United at present.

So no, the idea of Pochettino leaving the US so soon into his second term is hardly a shock. If it wasn’t to be United, or Tottenham, then he’d be a hot commodity if Real Madrid were to quickly abandon their reunion with Mourinho. If not them, then perhaps Milan again if their campaign were to sour before the festive season. And so on.

US Soccer deserves some credit for adequately preparing. For one thing, Pochettino’s retention was only made possible thanks to a billionaire super-donor, Ken Griffin. So while his wages dwarfed those of his predecessors, it hadn’t directly come at the expense of the federation’s other teams, initiatives or grassroots efforts.

The real boon is his release clause, a reported $10m (£7.5m) option that only a Big Club could afford to spring. Had Pochettino left after the World Cup, coach and federation would have parted with nothing more exchanged than a handshake and some pleasantries. Instead, they forged an insurance policy to make up for what could have been if Pochettino had stayed for a full cycle.

Of course, piles of money don’t qualify for World Cups. Should this international window be Pochettino’s last with the US, the onus will be on the federation to do what it couldn’t this summer and find an alternative to lead a program into an exciting new era. It would be a boon to the federation if that $10m pot was kept on standby to help foot the next coach’s wages, keeping the pool of possible candidates open and deep.

US Soccer will need to nail the next hire to reassure fans who fell for the team during their entertaining run at this year’s World Cup. That will probably be a project-by-committee, as the federation hasn’t seemed antsy to replace Matt Crocker after he quit his role as sporting director in April. And, if Pochettino was unlikely to be in the role all the way until 2030, perhaps it is a blessing that a split comes while the cycle is still dawning.

items.title: Firing a manager is often more about maintaining the illusion of control | Leander Schaerlaeckens
items.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
items.content:
In an era of advanced analytics, deciding when to move on from a manager still seems to come down to vibes rather than logic

His position had become untenable.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
In an era of advanced analytics, deciding when to move on from a manager still seems to come down to vibes rather than logic

He’d run out of time, out of credit, out of chances.

This time of year, we live in permanent peril of hearing some version of the above proclaimed with unshakable confidence. Some soccer manager has been fired and it is universally agreed that it had to be done, that there was no alternative, that the club’s hands were tied by circumstance.

It’s all a bit weird, this broadly accepted yet totally unscientific formula for when a manager must – MUST – lose his job. It’s a sort of alchemy of vibes, and results, and the absence of other scapegoats, and the alternatives available. It’s like that old definition of hardcore pornography by a US supreme court justice: I know it when I see it.

Shall we talk about Michael Carrick now? Yes, here is where we are obliged to debate the beleaguered Manchester United manager, who has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. There is almost total agreement on the latter point, that United’s issues are structural and systemic and absolve Carrick of blame. Still, he’s gotta go, because what can you do, eh?

By the time you read this, he may be gone, or about to be gone , or still floating around in the liminal vapors of being emotionally, but not yet physically, gone.

He was caretaker manager and did such a good job at that free-hit, can’t-lose gig – five stars! Clean and comfortable ride! – that he was rewarded with the exact same but altogether more difficult job of being the permanent Manchester United manager.

But the discourse has shifted against Carrick. Suddenly, the exact same skillset that helped him rescue United last season, making him a poster child of club DNA and its virtues, is viewed as deficient.

Now they say Carrick is outsmarted by the other managers, overwhelmed by the volume of games. Perhaps. But his tactical mind was up to it last year. With fewer games to worry about, certainly, but also burdened with Ruben Amorim’s debris to clear away first. Amorim, of course, was the predecessor who Simply Had To Go, because he was dogmatic and would need too much time to instill his methods, after he was hired because the club must have quite liked that he was dogmatic, even though he would need considerable time to instill his methods.

Yet hanging on to a manager often works out. There’s the famous case of Sir Alex Ferguson, of course, who was installed during United’s last flirtation with relegation, 40 years ago. The early years of his reign were not always smooth: he had a poor season in 1988-89 and was reportedly a few bad results from being sacked in January 1990. But he wasn’t, and nine years later, he was knighted for his accomplishments in management and, by extension, in not being fired.

It’s true of Mikel Arteta, too, who has teetered several times in charge of Arsenal. When the now-defending champions started the 2021-22 season without winning or scoring in three matches, including a 5-0 humiliation by Manchester City. And in late 2024. And as recently as this spring, when some felt that if Arteta didn’t deliver the title at last, he ought to be replaced. Six months on, that seems unthinkable.

There’s a graphic doing the rounds on social media showing that Carrick has actually done slightly better than Arteta in his first 27 league matches in charge, although this elides the very obviously opposite trajectories they were on. All the same, Arteta got to keep going; Carrick probably won’t. Few managers these days are allowed to grow on the job, or into it. The very things Ferguson once credited for his longevity – the leeway to evolve and develop and learn from his mistakes, to rebuild and retool – are denied to the managers supposed to succeed him. Because of … reasons? The money was different back then, but the pressure wasn’t .

Instead, that predictable thing has happened where Carrick has morphed from the in-fashion manager to the one who is gently mocked. He’s no longer said to look calm and possessed of the desperately needed poise at a tumultuous club. Now, he is described as glum. It seemed an ominous portent that he should add himself to the ultra-niche lore of English managers misusing umbrellas when he promised to hold the umbrella so that he would get wet and keep everyone else at the club dry, possibly owing to an unfamiliarity with the rudiments of the technology.

Carrick isn’t alone in managerial purgatory.

Crystal Palace’s Pierre Sage: sacked but somehow not yet sacked .

Régis Le Bris: safe for now, in spite of taking newly promoted Sunderland to an astounding seventh place last season.

Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle: medium rare, but not yet cooked.

Manchester City’s Enzo Maresca: definitely no longer the perfect successor to Pep Guardiola he was just a few weeks ago.

Fulham’s Álvaro Arbeloa and Bournemouth’s Marco Rose and Tottenham’s Roberto De Zerbi are fine now, after starting the season very not fine. That may change after any result at all. Because clubs’ decision-making on managers seems to be all just guesses and gambles. A veneer of deep deliberation is projected on to the process, because on the outside we always assume that soccer is more sophisticated than it is, but none of them really know which manager will perform in what situation, and for how long.

That’s amazing, given the advances in analytics and how much really rides on a manager’s ability to win games. Ballooning analytics departments seem to have taken teams to a place where they make far fewer mistakes in the transfer market than they used to.

Yet hiring a new manager, or firing the old one, or giving him another chance, appears to involve only marginally more design than shaking a Magic 8 Ball and seeing whether it endorses your choice.…

Coach’s contract has release clause of about $10m

United expected to sack Michael Carrick after awful start

US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

Securing Pochettino’s services is far from simple or inexpensive. The Argentinian’s contract contains a release clause in the neighborhood of $10m (£7.5m), multiple sources familiar with the deal told the Guardian this week, a figure that grows should United choose to retain Pochettino’s staff, including his longtime assistant and confidant Jesús Pérez, who has worked with Pochettino for 16 years. The Athletic first reported the details of Pochettino’s buyout.

Pochettino was brought on by the US in 2024 and guided the USMNT to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup , by most accounts a disappointment. US Soccer brought him back through 2030 , with both sides expressing a mutual belief and commitment towards not only brightening the fortunes of the US men but also overhauling the federation’s approach towards youth development.

“Every time we sign a contract, it’s to go to the last day of the contract,” Pochettino told reporters after his contract renewal. “If we sign a four-year contract, we need to think to arrive there. And we signed the contract because we really believe that we are going to be four years there. Because if not, it’s bad. If we don’t believe in that process, if we don’t believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice. It’s not the way that we think. We really signed that contract because we really believe that we can arrive to the end.”

Pochettino, who has been linked with a host of high-profile club openings since his arrival in the United States, tempered those remarks by adding another: “In life, nothing is sure. Less in football.”

The USMNT are days from a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches against Haiti in Cincinnati and Miami, their first competitive fixtures of the 2030 qualifying cycle. Pochettino is scheduled to address reporters on Friday afternoon.

Manchester United executives to settle head coach’s fate

Mauricio Pochettino a strong candidate to take over

Manchester United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, are expected to meet Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Tuesday and recommend the sacking of Michael Carrick.

Wilcox and Berrada have come to the conclusion that the 45-year-old should be removed as head coach after analysing his and the team’s performance.

They are poised to inform Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, that a new manager is needed, with Mauricio Pochettino emerging as a strong candidate.

Pochettino, the USA head coach, is open to the position and is believed to have a break clause that would require United to pay about £7m in compensation to the US Soccer Federation. The former Tottenham manager is contracted until the 2030 World Cup. Eddie Howe remains on Wilcox’s radar.

Carrick is due to take training on Tuesday with United in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League standings, having recorded three victories in 15 games in all competitions. Carrick came close to being removed after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October. But after Wilcox and Berrada met the following day at the training ground to discuss his position, Carrick was given the three games until the international break to prove he and the players could reverse a dismal start.

A defeat, a win and a draw in those matches and the displays in each, compounded with the overall run of form, have moved Wilcox and Berrada to a position where they are minded to remove Carrick. There is a growing expectation within the club that he will lose his job.

If Carrick is removed, Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a potential candidate as it is understood the USA head coach is open to the position, while sources indicate that Eddie Howe also remains on the radar of Wilcox too.

But after Wilcox and Berrada met the following day at the training ground to discuss his position, Carrick was given the three games until the international break to prove he and the players could reverse a dismal start.

A defeat, a win and a draw in those matches plus the team’s displays in each compounded with the overall run of form has moved Wilcox and Berrada towards a position where they are minded to remove Carrick. There is a growing expectation within the club that he will lose his job.

The final decision is yet to be made, though. When contacted on Monday night by the Guardian the club declined to comment.

In what may prove Carrick’s final three games in charge, United lost 2-0 at Chelsea , beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford and drew 4-4 at home against Villa on Sunday. In each game United were uneven. At Chelsea, Carrick’s side impressed in the first half but failed to convert chances before conceding twice after the interval, the second from a penalty after Lisandro Martínez was sent off.

In the Roma victory they were 2-0 behind in a poor opening 45 minutes before three goals in a rousing second one. On Sunday United twice trailed by two goals and entered added time 4-2 down, strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu rescuing a point.

After the Roma game Carrick urged his team to build momentum but within four minutes against Villa they were 2-0 down, continuing a pattern of conceding very early. In the 4-1 defeat at Como > last month, Nico Paz scored after two minutes. This followed Pablo Barrios’s opener one minute into the 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid > the previous week.

United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league

In Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league

I n Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

By the final whistle that wild 4‑4 draw at Old Trafford felt like a fitting endpoint to the opening quarter of the Premier League season. As we head into a 12‑day international break it is customary at this point to take a set of readings, to anatomise the season to date, to offer up a state of the Premier League address.

Five games since the last time we did this, not a great deal has changed. Brighton have maintained their luminous insurgent energy. The headline chart-breakers are Tottenham, up from second‑bottom to 11th. The official Home Office Spurs In Crisis threat level has been downgraded from Definitely In Crisis to Probably In Crisis A Bit Later On. Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar.

Otherwise there has been only one story in town across that autumn segment. And that story is Manchester, and the extraordinary contortions of two contrasting, but deeply conjoined mega-clubs.

Manchester City’s run from October to November kicked off with the guilty verdict on almost all of their financial charges, followed by an adrenal victory at Anfield, and finally a run of three problematic league defeats. United have basically fallen through the floor in the same period: played eight in all comps, won one, and a point off the bottom of the Premier League table.

At the same time both Manchester clubs have dominated the news cycle, inexhaustible content machines, and the source of football-adjacent stories so strange and so vast they threaten to surge up over the seawall and consume the rest of the league.

It is necessary at this point to talk about Michael Carrick and whether he has been sacked yet (current answer: no). It seems likely that this will happen in the current break, once the designated replacement has been lined up. Another Manchester United paradox: only here, in the realm of the mid-season panic-sacking do we suddenly feel ourselves in the hands of a slick and well-practised machine. Stand aside. We’re old hands at this. Leave it to the experts.

But Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.

Even the club executives captured by the TV pictures in insinuating close-up every week are essentially bit-part players, useful idiots for the regime: the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who looks every week a bit more like an office clerk trapped inside a hijacked foreign embassy trying to signal desperately with his eyes that he’s close to the edge and can someone in a flak jacket please appear at the fire escape window pretty soon. And the chief executive, Omar Berrada, who personally oversaw the Manchester City commercial sponsorship regime, and surely can’t be allowed to stay in his role at a listed company if the appeal against City’s charges is dismissed.

These are just the visible symptoms, not the cause. This is what happens when you run an institution where it is necessary to appoint people at significant levels who are willing to exist at a compromised level, who feel delighted to have the chance to run this organisation, even badly.

And by now it feels too easy to say the obvious thing. Manchester United have one competent but entirely self-motivated majority owner, for whom this has been a wonderful financial opportunity; and another owner whose only addition to the spectacle is to demonstrate the non‑transferable skills of the average billionaire.

We know this now. United are trapped in a cycle of self‑consumption. It is an ingrained, self-cannibalising decline, like a depressed post‑industrialised city in miniature. All that remains is rust, people and unspent heritage.

But it has also created something extraordinary in the past few weeks. Right now the Old Trafford match‑day atmosphere feels entirely unlike anything else, not just in sport but any other human activity at which you care to point.

The periphery is now enshrined definitively as The Event. Here is a man in sodden navy woollen menswear haunted by strange noises, striding the touchline like King Lear on his way to a golfing weekend. Here is the United crowd clamped together inside a clanky and leaking stadium, gripped by macro‑forces, shouting at the tides of power, a drama of alienation taking place just beyond the white lights around the lip of the stand.

The currents of energy are so mixed and nuanced. Who is cheering what? Where exactly is the love, the fear, the rage directed at this moment? Like all the best human dramas it is both sweeping and bathetic, thousands of human souls in that same shared space, all focused on an abstract idea, the act of faith and memory they identify collectively as Manchester United, while in front of them Harry Maguire trots about like an ageing police horse and Diogo Dalot attempts to play football with his legs on the wrong way round.…
